title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Explain the structural function of the physical assembly.
student: Based on the industrial application and the components shown, explain the primary structural function of the tie-rod assembly.
instructor: The assembly transfers axial load between connected parts while maintaining their relative spacing. The tie rod provides the tensile load path, while the surrounding tube provides a compressive load path to the supporting structure.

title: External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify how load enters the physical assembly.
student: Identify where the external load enters the assembly and describe its general direction relative to the tie rod.
instructor: The external load acts through the exposed end of the tie rod and is directed primarily along the longitudinal axis of the assembly.
gradingNotes: Students should describe the physical loading of the real system rather than use point labels from the later mechanics diagram.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Identify the physical restraint and the motion it prevents.
student: Identify where the assembly is restrained by the surrounding structure. What motion is prevented by this restraint?
instructor: The spacer tube bears against a rigid supporting structure. This support prevents axial motion at that end of the assembly and provides the reaction required to balance the applied axial load.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace force transfer through the rod, collar, tube, and support.
student: Trace the load path through the tie-rod assembly from the location where the external load is applied to the supporting structure.
instructor: The load enters through the steel tie rod, travels through the rod to the rigid collar, is transferred from the collar into the aluminum tube, and is then transferred from the tube into the supporting structure.

title: Member Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Recognize tension and compression from the physical load path.
student: Based on the load path, determine which major member is expected to experience tension and which is expected to experience compression. Explain physically why.
instructor: The steel rod is in tension because it is being pulled by the external load. The aluminum tube is in compression because the collar pushes the tube against the rigid support.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Recognize that both member deformations affect loaded-end movement.
student: If the engineering concern is the movement of the loaded end of the assembly, what deformation behavior of the individual members must be considered?
instructor: Both members must be considered. The steel rod elongates under tension, while the aluminum tube shortens under compression. Both changes influence the final position of the loaded end.
gradingNotes: This question introduces displacement compatibility conceptually without giving students the final displacement relationship.

title: Relevant Geometric and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the physical parameters governing axial deformation.
student: Identify the geometric, loading, and material characteristics that you expect to influence the axial deformation of the assembly.
instructor:
• Magnitude of the axial load.
  • Length of each deformable member.
  • Cross-sectional size of each member.
  • Stiffness of the steel material.
  • Stiffness of the aluminum material.
gradingNotes: At this stage students identify physical dependencies. Do not introduce the final deformation equation or instructor notation yet.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the physical assembly into a one-dimensional mechanics model.
student:
Convert the physical tie-rod assembly into a simplified one-dimensional Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the dominant axial load path. The model should show the steel rod, aluminum tube, rigid collar, supporting structure, externally applied axial load, and the geometric dimensions needed for axial-deformation analysis.

STUDENT MODEL / FREE-BODY DIAGRAM SPACE
instructor: A suitable idealization represents the system as coaxial axial members. The steel rod carries tensile force, the aluminum tube carries compressive force, the collar transfers load from the rod to the tube, and the tube transfers the load into the fixed support.
gradingNotes: Students do not need to reproduce the detailed industrial geometry. A clear one-dimensional idealization and free-body diagram are sufficient.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions supporting the axial-deformation model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real assembly into the simplified Mechanics of Materials model.
instructor:
• Loading is purely axial.
  • The steel rod and aluminum tube remain coaxial.
  • Materials behave linearly elastically.
  • Deformations are small.
  • The collar is rigid.
  • The supporting structure is rigid.
  • Axial stress is represented by its average value over each cross-section.
  • Local contact effects near the collar and support are neglected.
  • Local thread or attachment effects are neglected.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the mechanics steps needed to determine loaded-end displacement.
student: Before performing numerical calculations, describe the sequence of mechanics steps required to determine the displacement of the loaded end relative to the support.
instructor:
1. Determine the axial force carried by the steel rod.
  2. Determine the axial force carried by the aluminum tube.
  3. Determine the deformation of the aluminum tube.
  4. Determine how the tube deformation moves the collar relative to the fixed support.
  5. Determine the elongation of the steel rod.
  6. Combine the relative member displacements to determine the final displacement of the loaded end.

title: Boundary Condition and Member Action
learningObjectives: Identify the support condition and member actions in the reference model.
student: Using the instructor reference model, identify the boundary condition at A. State whether the steel rod and aluminum tube are in tension or compression.
instructor: The support at A prevents axial translation. The steel rod is in tension and the aluminum tube is in compression.

title: Internal Axial Forces
learningObjectives: Determine the internal axial force in each member.
student: Draw the required free-body diagrams and determine the internal axial force carried by the steel rod and the aluminum tube.
instructor: The steel rod carries Nst = +P = +{{axial_force_BC_kN}} kN in tension. The aluminum tube carries Nal = -P = {{axial_force_AB_kN}} kN in compression. The sign convention may vary if the physical tension/compression states are identified correctly.

title: Cross-Sectional Area of the Steel Rod
learningObjectives: Determine steel-rod area from its diameter.
student: Determine the cross-sectional area of the steel rod.
instructor:
For a circular rod, ABC = πdBC2/4. Using dBC = {{d_BC}} {{d_BC_unit}} gives

ABC = π({{d_BC}} mm)2/4 = {{axial_area_BC_mm2}} mm2.

title: Steel-Rod Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate the elongation of the steel rod.
student: Determine the axial elongation of the steel rod between the collar at B and the loaded end C.
instructor:
Using δ = NL/(AE),

δC/B = ({{axial_load_N}} N)({{L_BC}} mm) / [({{axial_area_BC_mm2}} mm2)({{axial_E_st_MPa}} N/mm2)]

δC/B = {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm to the right.

title: Aluminum-Tube Deformation
learningObjectives: Calculate the compressive deformation of the aluminum tube.
student: Determine the axial deformation of aluminum tube AB.
instructor:
Using compression as negative,

δAB = (-{{axial_load_N}} N)({{L_AB}} mm) / [({{A_AB}} mm2)({{axial_E_al_MPa}} N/mm2)]

δAB = -{{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm.

The tube therefore shortens by {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm.

title: Displacement of the Collar
learningObjectives: Relate tube shortening to the global displacement of the collar.
student: Use the shortening of the aluminum tube to determine the magnitude and direction of the displacement of collar B relative to the fixed support at A.
instructor:
Because A is fixed and the tube shortens, collar B moves toward the support. For the orientation shown, B moves {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm to the right.

δB/A = {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm to the right.
gradingNotes: This question separates member-deformation sign from global displacement direction.

title: Total Displacement of the Loaded End
learningObjectives: Combine member deformations to determine loaded-end displacement.
student: Determine the displacement of point C relative to the fixed support at A.
instructor:
The collar moves to the right because the aluminum tube shortens, and point C moves farther to the right relative to B because the steel rod elongates. The two contributions therefore add.

δC/A = δB/A + δC/B

δC/A = {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm + {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm = {{axial_total_displacement_mm}} mm ≈ {{axial_total_displacement_rounded_mm}} mm to the right.

title: Relative Contribution of the Two Members
learningObjectives: Compare the deformation contributions of the two members.
student: Compare the deformation contribution of the steel rod with that of the aluminum tube. Which member contributes more to the total displacement of the loaded end?
instructor: The steel rod contributes {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm, while the aluminum tube contributes {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm. The steel rod therefore contributes more. Although steel has a higher elastic modulus, the rod has a much smaller cross-sectional area and a greater effective length, producing the larger deformation contribution.

title: Stiffness-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Recommend geometric changes using axial stiffness.
student: Suppose the movement of the loaded end is larger than desired. Identify one geometric change to the steel rod and one geometric change to the aluminum tube that would reduce the total displacement. Explain your choices using axial stiffness.
instructor:
Axial stiffness is proportional to AE/L. Increasing the steel-rod diameter increases its area and reduces elongation. Increasing the aluminum-tube cross-sectional area reduces its compressive shortening. Reducing member length or using a material with a larger elastic modulus would also reduce deformation if permitted.

Axial stiffness ∝ AE/L.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Summarize the mechanical response and recommend a stiffness modification.
student: Summarize the mechanical response of the tie-rod assembly. State the predicted displacement of the loaded end, identify which member contributes most to that displacement, and recommend one modification if a stiffer assembly is required.
instructor: The loaded end moves approximately {{axial_total_displacement_rounded_mm}} mm to the right relative to the fixed support. About {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm comes from steel-rod elongation and {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm from aluminum-tube shortening. The steel rod contributes the larger share, so increasing the rod diameter is a direct mechanics-based modification for reducing total displacement.
